Pase lo que pase

You express “whatever happens” concession at B2 level with the reduplicated subjunctive (pase lo que pase, digan lo que digan, sea como sea, cueste lo que cueste, hagas lo que hagas) and with indefinites + subjunctive (dondequiera que, quienquiera que, cualquiera que, lo que sea, como quieras, cuando quieras).

To use the past variants: pasara lo que pasara, dijeran lo que dijeran.
To use the -quiera indefinites + que + subjunctive: dondequiera que, quienquiera que, cualquiera que.

The night before the exam

Friday, 10 July, ten in the evening, in Costel’s lorry cab. Tomorrow is the C1 exam. Mihai has just called: Grandpa Gheorghe has been taken to hospital with a high fever. Costel wants to give up the exam.
I’m going to the village tonight. I don’t care about the exam. One way or another, I’m not leaving Grandpa alone.
Costel, Grandpa isn’t alone. Mihai is with him, and Mihai’s a doctor. Whatever you do, you won’t help more than he can.
Besides, we’ve been preparing for a year. Whatever anyone says, tomorrow we have to be there.
And what if something happens to him while I’m in the exam? I’d never forgive myself.
Mihai has just called. Grandpa wants to talk to you. Here.
(on the phone) Grandpa? … Yes. … Yes, sir. … As you wish. … OK. … Por fin. Salud.
What did he say?
That whatever happens, I’m going to the exam. That whoever stays at home because of him will have him to deal with.
Anything else?
That whatever it takes, in August he turns ninety-seven, and he wants to celebrate with my C1 diploma hanging on the wall.

1. The reduplicated structure
The subjunctive verb is repeated, linked by “lo que”, “como”, “donde”, “cuando” or “quien”. It means “whatever / however / wherever it may be”:
verb + lo que + verb
Pase lo que pase, tú vas al examen.
verb + como + verb
Sea como sea, se pondrá bien.
verb + donde + verb
Vayas donde vayas, llévate el libro.
wherever you go
verb + quien + verb
Venga quien venga, la puerta está abierta.
whoever comes
verb + lo que + verb (amount)
Cueste lo que cueste, lo celebraremos.
2. In the past
Whatever happened, he always switched on the lamp at seven.
Whatever people said, he didn’t close the bookshop until 1994.
However it was, she always went back to Madrid in her books.
When you narrate in the past, both verbs change to the imperfect subjunctive: pase lo que pase → pasara lo que pasara.
3. Dondequiera que, quienquiera que, cualquiera que
Wherever it is published, the cover will be the same.
Whoever stays at home because of me will have me to deal with.
Whichever book you choose will be fine.
Anyone who knows him will tell you the same.
“Cualquiera” becomes “cualquier” before a noun: cualquier libro, cualquier día. The plural “cualesquiera” is very rare and formal.

That year, July arrived in Bucharest with a heatwave that emptied the streets from midday until seven in the evening. Rosa Elena had gone to the village with her grandmother Elena as soon as kindergarten finished, to spend the summer with Grandpa Gheorghe, under the walnut tree. She had promised Ecaterina she would send her a photo every day. And she did, every day at seven: the walnut tree, the well, the hens, Grandpa asleep on the porch after lunch with his mouth open, Grandpa annoyed because the little girl had photographed him asleep after lunch with his mouth open.

Faustino, meanwhile, was still in Seville. He had gone for a week at the end of June, and in July he still hadn’t come back. He had asked Lucas, Andrei’s colleague, to look after his stall on the Cuesta de Moyano at weekends. Lucas, who had never sold a book in his life, discovered he loved it. On Sundays he sat on Faustino’s stool, in a borrowed beret, and told customers the story of La Lámpara, the plaque and the five-hundred-peseta note, with so many invented details that Faustino, when he heard, said he was going to hire him.

Ecaterina, in Bucharest, spent her mornings correcting the proofs of “Lampa aprinsă”, the Romanian edition, wearing Andrés’s tortoiseshell glasses. It was so hot that she worked with her feet in a basin of cold water, as her mother had taught her in the summers of the fifties. In the evenings, at seven, she switched on the little lamp in the living room, even though it was still daylight. She hadn’t missed a single evening since 18 June. Rosa Elena, from the village, asked her by message every day whether she had switched it on yet. Ecaterina always answered with a photo.

Costel and Señor Dan’s C1 exam was on Saturday 11 July. On Friday the 10th, at ten at night, the two of them were in the lorry cab, parked outside Señor Dan’s block, going over things one last time, although Ana had forbidden them to study the night before. Ana had come to bring them sandwiches and to check they weren’t studying. She found them studying. Before she could scold them, her phone rang. It was Mihai, from the village. He was speaking fast and quietly, in the doctor’s voice he used when something was wrong.

Grandpa Gheorghe had had a high fever since the afternoon, and was finding it hard to breathe. Mihai, who had gone to the village for the weekend, had listened to his chest with a stethoscope and hadn’t liked what he heard at all. He suspected pneumonia. At ninety-six, he explained to Ana, pneumonia was no joke. They had called an ambulance, which would take an hour to get there along the village roads, and they were going to take him to the district hospital. Rosa Elena was awake, very frightened, clinging to her grandmother Elena.

Mihai also explained that Grandpa, despite the fever, still had a terrible temper. He had refused to get into the ambulance until Elena brought him his Sunday cap, because he said that, whatever happened, he wasn’t going into a hospital with his hair a mess. And before they closed the ambulance door, he had asked Rosa Elena to light the oil lamp in the window at seven, in case he didn’t get back in time. The little girl had promised to light it every night, whatever it took.

Costel heard it all on speaker. He snapped his book shut, took off his reading glasses and said he was going to the village that very night, in the lorry if need be. That he didn’t care about the exam. That, one way or another, he wasn’t leaving Grandpa alone. Ana reminded him that Grandpa wasn’t alone: Mihai was with him, and Mihai was a doctor. Whatever Costel did, he wouldn’t help more than his doctor grandson. Señor Dan added that they had been preparing for that exam for a year, and that, whatever anyone said, the next day they had to be at the Instituto Cervantes at nine.

Costel wasn’t convinced. He said that if something happened to Grandpa while he was sitting in a classroom talking about climate change, he would never forgive himself. Ana didn’t know what to say to him. Half an hour later the phone rang again. It was Mihai once more. The ambulance had arrived. Grandpa, on the stretcher, with an oxygen mask, had asked to speak to Costel. Mihai had told him it wasn’t the moment. Grandpa had taken off his mask and said, with what little voice he had left, that it was.

While they waited, Señor Dan took out of his pocket the table he had prepared for the exam, the last one, with the C1 connectors arranged by colour. He looked at it for a moment and then tore it into four pieces, very slowly. Costel and Ana looked at him in surprise. Señor Dan explained that, whatever the books say, at eleven o’clock the night before you don’t learn anything, and the only thing you can do is wait with someone beside you. Then he fell silent, with the pieces of the table in his hand, looking at Ana’s phone.

Ana handed the phone to Costel. Costel listened for a whole minute, saying almost nothing: “Yes… Yes, sir… As you wish… OK.” At the end, Grandpa said something else, and Costel answered, in Spanish: “Por fin. Salud.” Then he hung up. His eyes were red. Señor Dan asked him what he had said. Costel answered that Grandpa had told him that, whatever happened, he should go to the exam. That whoever stayed at home because of him would have him to deal with. And that, whatever it took, in August he intended to turn ninety-seven with a C1 diploma hanging on the wall.

That night, none of the three slept. Ana stayed awake in the kitchen, with her phone on the table, waiting for news from the hospital. Señor Dan went over irregular verbs in his head until four. Costel stayed in the lorry cab, with the ceiling light on, as on 18 June. At five in the morning a message came from Mihai: Grandpa was in hospital, on antibiotics and oxygen, and the fever had started to come down. He was stable. He had asked for soup. The doctors had refused. He had got angry. Mihai wrote that this was a very good sign.

Before leaving home, Costel called his daughter in Valencia. She already knew everything, because Ana had written to her at midnight. She told him she was proud of him, whatever the result. Then she passed the phone to Álex, who told him, in his school Spanish, that he was going to “eat it with chips”. Costel didn’t understand the expression. Álex explained it meant he was going to do brilliantly. Costel wrote it on a piece of paper and put it in his shirt pocket, next to Rosa Elena’s drawing, in case he needed it in the oral.

At a quarter to nine, Costel and Señor Dan were outside the Instituto Cervantes. Costel was wearing his special-occasions shirt, unironed, and Señor Dan, for the first time in his life, had only one pen. Ana had come to see them off at the door. She gave each of them an envelope, as in November. Inside was a drawing Rosa Elena had made that very morning at the hospital, while waiting to be allowed to see Grandpa: a lorry, a bridge and, in the middle, a very old man in a bed, giving a thumbs-up. Underneath, in Romanian, it said: “Bunicul zice: mergeți.”

The C1 exam was much harder than the B2. The texts were newspaper articles full of irony, the recordings were radio debates in which four people talked at once, and written expression asked for an argumentative essay on the loneliness of elderly people in cities. Costel read the topic and sat still for a moment. Then he began to write without stopping. He wrote about a ninety-six-year-old man who, from a stretcher, with an oxygen mask, had ordered a family friend not to stay at home because of him. He wrote it in the third person, without names. But anyone who read it would have understood who he was talking about.

Señor Dan, for his part, chose the other topic in written expression: an opinion piece on whether cities should ban cars from the centre. He planned it as always, like a bridge, but this time it didn’t come out so neatly. He said afterwards that halfway through the second paragraph he had remembered Grandpa on the stretcher and lost the thread for five minutes. In the end he had finished the text with a sentence that wasn’t in any table: “One way or another, cities belong to those who live in them, not to those who rush through them.”

The oral test was in the afternoon. Costel got a very young examiner from Valladolid, who asked him which tradition from his country he found most interesting. Costel told her about the lamps of 18 June: about a six-year-old girl who had come up with the idea of everyone switching on a light at the same time, and about the lorry drivers in five countries who had done it without knowing who for. The examiner told him that wasn’t a Romanian tradition. Costel replied that it wasn’t yet, but that, whatever happened, it would be. The examiner smiled and wrote something on her sheet.

When they came out of the exam, at six, Costel and Señor Dan didn’t go to celebrate. They got into Señor Dan’s car and drove three hours to the district hospital. They arrived at nine at night. Grandpa Gheorghe was sitting up in bed, with an oxygen tube in his nose, complaining that the hospital dinner had no salt. When he saw Costel come in, the first thing he asked, even before greeting him, was how the exam had gone. Costel told him he didn’t know. Grandpa replied that this was a good sign, because those who know always fail.

Rosa Elena was asleep in an armchair in the room, with her camera in her hands. She had spent the whole day at the hospital, photographing Grandpa, the doctors, the nurses, the soup they wouldn’t let him eat. When she woke up and saw Costel, she burst into tears of relief, because nobody had explained to her that Grandpa was already better and she had spent the day thinking the worst. Costel picked her up. He told her Grandpa was stronger than a lorry. Rosa Elena answered that that was what Zoltán said, and it made no sense at all.

Before they left, very late, Grandpa asked to be alone with Costel for a moment. The others went out into the corridor. Nobody ever knew exactly what he told him. Costel only said, years later, that Grandpa had taken his hand and told him he had learnt to read at thirty, in the army, because as a child he had had to look after the sheep, and nobody had ever given him a diploma for it. “So I’ll hang yours,” he had said. “Whatever it takes.”

Grandpa spent ten days in hospital. The doctors said it was an extraordinary case for his age, and he replied that what was extraordinary was that they wouldn’t let him have a single drop of țuică. Mihai stayed with him almost the whole time, sleeping on a chair. Elena brought him soup on the sly, in a flask, and he drank it very quickly, watching the door. Rosa Elena showed him the day’s photos and explained in Spanish what was in each one. Grandpa didn’t understand a thing, but said “por fin” to every photo, and the little girl laughed.

Ana, who had gone back to Bucharest to work, went to see Ecaterina at the end of the week and told her all about the hospital. Ecaterina listened in silence. Then she said Grandpa Gheorghe and Andrés would have got on very well, because they both had the same way of not giving up: without making a fuss and without asking permission. Ana asked whether she meant Andrés waiting forty years. Ecaterina said no, she meant Andrés switching on the lamp every evening at seven, whatever happened, even if nobody was going to come in.

Meanwhile, in Madrid, Ecaterina got a call from Inés. She said she had two pieces of news, one good and one very good, and didn’t know which to start with. Ecaterina told her to start with whichever she liked. Inés started with the good one: the third edition of “La lámpara encendida” was already in the bookshops. Then the very good one: a publisher in Turin had bought the translation rights, and another in Lisbon was interested. Ecaterina fell silent. Inés asked whether she was still there. Ecaterina said yes, she was thinking of Andrés, who didn’t know a word of Italian.

Inés asked whether she wanted to set any conditions for the translations. Ecaterina thought for a moment. Then she said just one: that wherever the book was published, in whatever language, the cover should be the same, Andrei’s empty drawer. And that the photographer’s name should always appear on the flap. Inés said that would be hard to negotiate with some publishers. Ecaterina replied that she could negotiate it however she liked, but that, whatever it took, that photo was not to be changed. Inés laughed and said she sounded just like Begoña.

On 20 July, Andrei got a message from Faustino in Seville. It was the longest message Faustino had ever written, and it had only three mistakes. He told him that the day before, under the orange tree in doña Remedios’s courtyard, he had asked her to marry him. He hadn’t got down on his knees, because she had warned him that if he knelt down he wouldn’t be able to get up again, and then people really would have something to say. Doña Remedios had said yes. That whatever her grandchildren and the neighbours in Triana said, at their age there was no time to lose.

Doña Remedios, for her part, wrote Ecaterina a real letter, by hand, which arrived in Bucharest a week later. She told her that her daughter had said nobody got married at her age, and that she had replied that, one way or another, at her age you weren’t waiting for anything either, and she had waited long enough. She asked her to come to the wedding, however she could and with whoever she wanted. And to bring the book, because she intended to put it on the altar, next to the flowers. Ecaterina read the letter on the balcony, at seven, with the lamp lit behind her.

The wedding would be in October, in Triana, in a small church near the river. Faustino wanted Andrei to take the photos, whatever happened. And he asked him to tell Lucas to keep the stall on the Cuesta de Moyano for as long as it took, because he didn’t know when he would be back in Madrid, or whether he would be back at all. Andrei read the message aloud in the hallway of the flat on the calle del Prado, in front of the green sign. Marta, who was in the kitchen, dropped a cup on the floor. Then she ran to her notebook and wrote a single word on the last page: “Ending.”

When Lucas heard, he was so pleased that he closed the stall for an hour to go and celebrate at the bar opposite, and sold four books when he got back, more than he had sold all month. Begoña told him that if he wanted to go on being a bookseller at weekends, she had nothing against it, as long as he was at the agency at nine on Monday. Lucas asked whether that was a yes. Begoña answered: “Do what you like, but do it well.” Lucas said it was the closest thing to a blessing she had ever given him.

On 21 July, Grandpa Gheorghe left hospital. Mihai drove him to the village, very slowly, stopping every half hour so Grandpa could stretch his legs. When they arrived, Grandpa refused to go to bed. He sat on the porch, under the walnut tree, asked for soup with salt and, when night fell, at seven o’clock sharp, lit the oil lamp in the window facing the road, as on 18 June. Elena asked him who he was lighting it for. Grandpa told her for everyone who had stayed awake for him. And that, from that day on, he would light it every night, whatever happened.

At the end of July, Costel went back to the village with his lorry, loaded with things Grandpa didn’t need: a fan, a new radio, a crate of oranges from Valencia that his daughter had sent him and a jar of zacuscă from Mrs Florica. He sat with Grandpa on the porch, under the walnut tree, at lamp time. Grandpa asked him when the C1 results came out. Costel told him in September or October. Grandpa said he had plenty of time, then, to hang the diploma before his birthday next year. Costel reminded him that his birthday was in August. Grandpa replied that he knew, but that, one way or another, he intended to turn ninety-eight as well.

Before he left, Costel asked Grandpa what he wanted for his birthday. Grandpa thought for a long time, looking at the oil lamp. Then he told him he wanted just one thing: that in August everyone should come to the village, the ones from Bucharest, Madrid and Seville, and sit under the walnut tree, like the summer before. Costel asked whether he wanted Faustino to come too. Grandpa answered yes, he wanted to meet a man who was getting married at eighty-seven, because maybe he would give him ideas.
